title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Page 102-103 (sections XIII-XVI start) of E297, Novi Commentarii 10 (1764, publ. 1766). Euler is recasting his 1744 Methodus inveniendi analytically, following Lagrange's delta-algorithm. He wants to extremize A = ∫_0^a Z dx.

XIII. Every ordinate y(x) receives an infinitely small, arbitrary increment δy. These increments are independent of one another and of the values of y. Euler contrasts two configurations of the integral. The 'status principalis' is the sought extremal relation y(x). The 'status variatus' is y+δy at the same x. Extremality requires that the difference between the two states vanish. Euler stresses the distinction between dy, the change along the curve as x→x+dx, and δy, the change from curve to neighbouring curve at fixed x. In modern terms δy = εη(x) is a variation, or tangent vector in function space, with x not varied.

XIV. δZ denotes the increment of any function Z at a given x when passing to the varied state. If Z depends on x alone, δZ = 0, since x is not varied. Euler announces three cases, according as Z contains:
- only x and y;
- also the ratio of differentials p = dy/dx, etc.;
- integral formulas.

XV. Case 1, Z = Z(x,y). Substituting y→y+δy gives δZ = N δy, where dZ = M dx + N dy. That is, δ is the ordinary differential with dx→0 and dy→δy; modern form δZ = Z_y δy.

XVI (continued on the next page). Then δA = ∫ N δy dx. Because δy is arbitrary, N = ∂Z/∂y = 0 pointwise. This is the degenerate Euler-Lagrange equation for an integrand without derivatives. Euler notes it holds whatever the upper limit a, since the condition is pointwise.
errors: No mathematical errors. The argument 'arbitrary δy ⇒ integrand vanishes' (completed on the next page) is the fundamental lemma used without proof, as was standard in 1764. The degenerate case N=0 gives a pointwise extremum condition; Euler does not remark that this is not an extremum over curves in any interesting sense, nor discuss max vs. min.

ideas.what: Distinction between the principal and the varied state, and between d (along the curve) and δ (between curves at fixed x), with arbitrary independent variations δy of all ordinates simultaneously
ideas.modern_name: First variation / variational operator δ; Gateaux derivative in direction η
ideas.usually_credited_to: J.-L. Lagrange (letter to Euler 1755; Miscellanea Taurinensia 1760-61); named and systematized by Euler (E296 Elementa calculi variationum, E297)
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum (Novi Comm. 10, 1766) and this paper E297; later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385); Opera omnia I.25 introduction by Carathéodory

ideas.what: Rule: δZ is obtained from dZ by setting dx=0 and dy=δy; δZ = Nδy for Z(x,y)
ideas.modern_name: Partial derivative / chain rule for the first variation

ideas.what: Remark that the reworked method (all ordinates varied at once) contains the earlier 1744 method (one ordinate varied) as a special case, and is motivated by the 'principle of continuity'
ideas.modern_name: Variations with compact/arbitrary support vs. local 'needle' variation of one ordinate
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's own historical self-assessment; discussed by Carathéodory (OO I.24/25), Goldstine (History of the Calculus of Variations, 1980), Fraser
ideas.where_published: E297 sections X-XII; Goldstine 1980; Fraser's papers on Euler and Lagrange's variational calculus

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard, well-documented exposition of the Lagrange-Euler δ-calculus (state principal vs. varied, d vs. δ, δZ = Nδy). It is thoroughly covered by Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction, Goldstine and Fraser. Nothing new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription agrees well with the image; only the long-s typography is normalized. The page ends with the catchword 'particula' (split 'par-/ticula' across pages), consistent with the next page.
